chapter_theme: The wife as the household's real wealth. The chapter praises her steadfastness and even grants her power over the rain, yet it is told largely from the husband's side, and it measures her by what she makes possible for his life.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's notes divide it: her qualities and fit with his income (51), that only her worth matters to household life (52-53), steadfastness and its power (54-55), steadfastness and its protection (56-57), her reward (58), the husband's shame without it (59), and a bridge to children (60).

51.reading: She who has the excellence the home needs, and lives within the means of the man who took her, is the companion of life.
51.nuance: Income literacy is half the definition, and it comes before chastity is mentioned. Parimelazhagar makes her skills concrete: knowing what is needed, cooking and neighbourly help. Manakkudavar instead reads மனை as her birth family, which shifts the standard from her work to where she comes from.

52.reading: If the wife lacks household excellence, the life has nothing, whatever other distinction it may have.
52.nuance: The final word இல், nothing, is blunt. The verse doesn't say the life is worse, it says the life isn't there at all, and Parimelazhagar says this is because it bears no fruit.

53.reading: What is lacking if the wife has worth, and what is present if she does not?
53.nuance: Two questions with no answers given. Manakkudavar supplies the sharp version: though the man has nothing, nothing is lacking, and though he has everything, nothing is there.

54.reading: What is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு?
54.nuance: The word திண்மை presents கற்பு as a strength, not as mere purity. Whether the verse is ranking a possession or a form of life is what divides the commentators.

positions.position: A wife is ranked among the things a man can obtain, and none is better.
positions.quote: ஒருவன் எய்தும் பொருள்களுள் இல்லாளின் மேம்பட்ட பொருள்கள் யாவை உள

positions.position: The comparison is about being born a woman, which nothing exceeds if it has this firmness.
The firmness is womanhood's own strength of character.

55.reading: She who rises worshipping her husband and not a god: if she says 'rain', it rains.
55.nuance: The verse says flatly that she doesn't worship a god. Parimelazhagar softens this by adding 'other' gods. The line is both the strongest claim of a woman's power in the book and the most troubling, and Kalaignar's entry reads the rain as an image of fearful servitude, not of power.

positions.position: Her husband is her own god, and her steadfastness is so powerful that the deities obey her.
positions.quote: பிற தெய்வம் தொழாது தன் தெய்வம் ஆகிய கொழுநனைத் தொழாநின்று துயிலெழுவாள்

positions.position: She regards all gods as being her husband.
Such a wife is like rain falling in fear at a command: she has made herself a slave.

56.reading: She is a woman who guards herself, cares for the man who took her, keeps their good name and does not flag.
56.nuance: பெண் here is a title that has to be earned, as the verse defines who counts as a woman. Parimelazhagar takes சொல் as a shared reputation for wife and husband, which means she is responsible for both.

57.reading: What use is the guarding of women by confinement? The guard that their own steadfastness keeps is the best.
57.nuance: The verse rejects confinement because it does not work, and it doesn't speak of the woman's rights. It leaves in place the assumption that she needs guarding, but it moves that guard inside her.

positions.position: Walls and door-guards are useless without நிறை, the holding of her heart to chastity.
positions.quote: காவல் இரண்டினும் நிறைக் காவல் இல்வழி ஏனைச் சிறைக்காவலால் பயன் இல்லை

positions.position: The verse is a charge against men: treating such women as slaves is ignorance.

58.reading: If women obtain the one who obtained them, they will gain great distinction in the world where the gods live.
58.nuance: The word play பெற்றாற் பெறின் leaves open what 'obtaining' a husband means. Who has to be worthy depends on how the gap is filled.

positions.position: The missing word is worship: women who serve their husbands are honoured by the gods.
If a woman obtains a virtuous husband, household life becomes a new world for her.

59.reading: Those whose home does not seek renown cannot walk with a great beast's proud gait before those who deride them.
59.nuance: The man's public bearing is said to depend on his wife's conduct. ஏறு needn't mean a lion as Pope and Parimelazhagar have it, since the word covers male animals generally, and Manakkudavar describes the gait without naming an animal.

60.reading: They call a home's excellence its blessing, and good children its fine ornament.
60.nuance: Parimelazhagar says this verse prepares for the next chapter by naming the wife's ornament. Children are ornaments here and do not yet have the value they get in chapter 7. Kalaignar takes மனைமாட்சி as the family's culture and not specifically the wife's.

links.note: Verse 9 calls a head that does not bow to the Lord's feet useless. Here a woman who does not worship a god is the one whom the rain obeys. Parimelazhagar's added 'other gods' softens the contrast, but the Tamil does not contain it.
In 18, even the gods' worship depends on rain. Here rain answers to a woman who bypasses the gods. Together the two verses invert the expected order of gods, rain and humans.

The wife lives within her husband's income, and 478 applies the same rule to the king's treasury: a small inflow is no ruin if outflow doesn't widen. The Kural's household economics and statecraft share one rule.

Here நிறை is the guard that outdoes all confinement. In 1251, speaking as a woman in love, desire's axe breaks the door of நிறை barred with shame. The book's ethics section treats inner guard as sufficient, and its love section knows it isn't.

source_issues: Kalaignar's entry for verse 55 continues with text about his commentary ('கலைஞரின் நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலத்துக்கு'), so it appears to be taken from a secondary essay. Only its first sentence is used here, and it should be checked against his own commentary.
The Tamil of verse 51 in kg/core reads மனைக்தக்க, a typo for மனைத்தக்க.
Manakkudavar's entry for verse 60 opens with a fragment of the verse and ends with a stray '10'.
